hints: Remember boiling breaks the forces between molecules, not the strong covalent bonds inside them, so focus on intermolecular forces.
Notice both molecules have the same $M_r$ of 28 and the same total electron count of 14, so their London dispersion forces will be very similar.
Compare their polarity to see which one gets an extra dipole-dipole attraction on top of dispersion, giving it the slightly higher boiling point.
walkthrough:
**What controls boiling point?**

Boiling separates molecules from each other. It overcomes intermolecular forces, it does not break covalent bonds.

So we compare: $\text{intermolecular forces in } \text{N}_2 \text{ vs } \text{CO}$

**Rule out size and electrons**

Both have $M_r = 28$. Let's count electrons:
$$\text{N}_2: 7+7 = 14 \text{ electrons}$$
$$\text{CO}: 6+8 = 14 \text{ electrons}$$
With the same mass and same electrons, London dispersion forces are almost identical. That cannot explain the difference.

**Check polarity for extra forces**

$\text{N}_2$ is non-polar with symmetrical sharing, so it has London forces only. $\text{CO}$ is polar because C and O have different electronegativities, so it has a permanent dipole.

That means $\text{CO}$ has London forces plus permanent dipole-dipole forces, which need a little more energy to break. Hence the higher boiling point of 82 K versus 77 K.

options.A: Correct. CO is polar and has permanent dipole-dipole attractions in addition to London forces, while non-polar N2 has London forces only. Stronger total intermolecular forces means more energy to separate CO molecules, so higher boiling point.
options.B: Incorrect. Both molecules have multiple bonding with sigma and pi components. CO is isoelectronic with N2 and has a triple bond (one sigma, two pi), not sigma only. Intramolecular bonding also does not determine boiling point.
options.C: Incorrect. This confuses intramolecular with intermolecular forces. Boiling does not break the N triple bond or the C-O bond. Also CO does not have a simple C=O double bond, it has a triple bond similar in strength to N2.
options.D: Incorrect. Count the electrons: N has 7, so N2 has 14. C has 6 and O has 8, so CO also has 14. With equal electrons and equal Mr, London forces are very similar, so this cannot explain the 5 K difference.
